<reason>Side B (PRO) won on the strength of direct, labeled answers to pressure and cleaner resolution of the central clash. A's strongest line — that PRO kept defending a weight/hood-height schedule rather than the motion as written — was genuinely sharp, but B defused it: the motion's own conditional ("when their size imposes higher safety and street-use costs") makes the fee cost-keyed, and B answered the three-ton sedan question with a plain "Yes," then exploited A's concession that cost-keyed pricing would be acceptable, reducing A's case to a label complaint. B also neutralized the exposure attack by noting that parking and curb fees (two of the motion's three instruments) charge per use per foot, matching the fuel-tax standard A praised, and answered the earmark complaint with the standard price-signal point. A's regressivity and confounder points were answered in B's first rebuttal (unpriced risk is regressive; confounds don't repeal biomechanics) and never re-established as live. Both sides used plausible background knowledge (Paris, fourth-power rule) without fake precision, and both formatted Q/A rounds correctly. A's rhetoric ("penalty wearing a spreadsheet," the tribe verdict) was memorable and kept this competitive, but B made the debate easier to decide and closed the cleaner path to victory.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>The decisive exchange was A's pressure Q1 (does a three-ton EV sedan pay the same fee?) meeting B4.1's direct "Yes" plus the geometry explanation — B's answer not only honored the motion's cost-conditional text but trapped A, whose later concession that cost-keyed pricing "is a bill I'd debate on the merits" let B shrink the entire dispute to a label difference in the closing.</best_rebuttal>
